source.title: Error-Bounded Correction of Noisy Labels
source.authors: Songzhu Zheng; Pengxiang Wu; A. Goswami; Mayank Goswami; Dimitris N. Metaxas; Chao Chen

record.file_problem: The supplied paper text and supplementary material are present; some equations and table layout are flattened, but the document is readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper presents results about label-noise memorization as context, then tests a different question: whether confidence from a noisy-label classifier can identify and correct corrupted labels. It does not test the claim's listed behaviors as stated; related findings and limitations refine their scope.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Zhang et al. (2017) for strong memorization power and Arpit et al. (2017) for learning meaningful patterns before overfitting, but these are prior-work claims, not this study's results. Its own empirical results evaluate noisy-label detection/correction and classifier accuracy under injected noise. They do not measure fitting fully random labels, fitting unstructured inputs, training-time ratios, performance as corruption rises from none to all, regularization's necessity/sufficiency, or learning order of true versus random labels. Therefore no result rows bear on V1–V6. The CIFAR10 confidence-bound experiment and tabulated classifier accuracies are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The Standard baseline supplies original evidence relevant to V6: on CIFAR10 with 40% uniform noise, the authors describe later overfitting to noisy labels accompanied by declining clean-test performance (Section 4, Figure 3). Table 2 also tests V4's test-performance component across intermediate corruption levels. The record incorrectly excludes these baseline results along with the method evaluations.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors derive conditional guarantees connecting noisy-classifier predictions to label correctness and propose LRT-based correction, reporting improved robustness across datasets. Their guarantees concern agreement with the Bayes-optimal classifier under stated assumptions.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes iterative likelihood-ratio label correction during training; it does not reproduce the original random-label memorization experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise pattern and noise level vary across the reported benchmark results; the confidence-bound experiment is conducted on CIFAR10 with symmetric and asymmetric noise at 20%.

fits_no_version.finding: The CIFAR10 confidence-bound experiments assess agreement with an estimated Bayes-optimal decision and identification of corrupted labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Classifier confidence can identify unreliable labels under the stated assumptions.

fits_no_version.finding: AdaCorr and other mitigation methods are compared through test accuracy after modifying training or correcting labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Label-noise mitigation can improve generalization on the tested datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: The synthetic Gaussian-mixture experiments validate confidence and correction bounds using known conditional probabilities.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The proposed bounds hold empirically in a structured Gaussian-mixture classification problem.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 119 (2020)
record.problems: The CIFAR10 confidence-bound evidence is presented in figures without extractable numerical values in the text. The authors approximate the clean conditional probabilities using a neural network. The multiclass correction guarantee includes an error term for cases where the Bayes-optimal class is neither the observed label nor the classifier's predicted class; the supplementary proof describes this case as not properly handled. Table 2 is flattened, making reliable assignment of all cells to conditions difficult. The Clothing 1M accuracy conflicts between prose (71.47%) and Table 1 (71.74 ± 0.12).
record.rows_left_out: No rows were extracted because the study's own results do not measure any of V1–V6. Table 2's noisy-label benchmark accuracies and the CIFAR10 confidence-bound figures concern label-noise robustness or label purity, not the claim versions; their mappings and values are not fully recoverable from the flattened/figure-only presentation.

untested.parts: Completely random labels, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged training hyperparameters.
Training-time ratios and convergence slowdown as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or unstructured Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit across corruption levels; clean and completely randomized endpoints; convergence of test error to chance.
Whether explicit regularization prevents random-label fitting and whether removing it harms clean-label generalization.
Separate learning curves for clean and corrupted training examples, fully random-label comparisons, and generality beyond the reported Standard convergence example.

missing.what: Standard training accuracy against noisy labels and clean-test accuracy over training at 40% uniform noise. Record the authors' qualitative late-overfitting result; numerical curve values are unavailable in the supplied text.
missing.locator: Section 4, Discussion; Figure 3, right panel and caption

record.verdict_notes: Table 2's Standard noise-sweep results were declared in rows_left_out, so they are not listed again as missing. Their exclusion as irrelevant should be corrected: they bear on V4's test-degradation component. Figure 3's baseline result was overlooked. Neither result establishes perfect training interpolation. The supplied text contains captions and discussion but no readable numerical Figure 3 curves.

versions.untested_parts: No experiment on completely random labels, training error on them, test error at chance, or unchanged architecture/hyperparameters.
No comparison of training time for true versus random labels or convergence time by corruption fraction.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input fitting experiments.
No sweep from zero to complete random corruption measuring perfect training fit and steadily changing test error.
No test of whether weight decay, dropout, or augmentation prevent random-label fitting or whether their removal harms true-label generalization.
No measurement of whether the networks learn shared real-data patterns before memorizing noisy or random labels.

relationships.condition: Standard training with uniform flipping at reported noise levels 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, and 0.8
relationships.reason: From Table 2 text, Standard test accuracy decreases monotonically: MNIST 99.0→91.3%, CIFAR10 87.5→47.6%, CIFAR100 58.9→20.8%, and ModelNet40 79.1→57.9%. This supports the test-degradation component only; no linked rows were extracted.
relationships.display_finding: Test accuracy declined monotonically from 99.0% to 91.3% on MNIST, 87.5% to 47.6% on CIFAR10, 58.9% to 20.8% on CIFAR100, and 79.1% to 57.9% on ModelNet40.

relationships.condition: Standard ResNet-34 training on CIFAR10 with 40% uniform label noise
relationships.reason: Section 4's discussion of Figure 3 explicitly describes noisy-label overfitting and subsequent clean-test degradation, qualitatively supporting signal learning before noise memorization. This verdict uses the text; the convergence result has no extracted rows.
relationships.display_finding: Overfitting to noisy labels was followed by declining accuracy on clean test data.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
